title: Beyond Frameworks: Unpacking Collaboration Strategies in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Existing multi-agent LLM frameworks focus on architecture and role assignment, leaving the fine-grained mechanics of collaboration, such as how agents govern interactions, when they communicate, and how much dialogue context they share, underexplored. The paper formalizes four dimensions: governance (centralized, with an instructor agent coordinating, versus decentralized self-organization), participation per discussion round (full versus selective), interaction pattern (broadcast, targeted peer messages, or simultaneous versus sequential turns), and context management (full dialogue history versus summarized history). These strategies are tested on two scenarios, Distributed Evidence Integration (DEI) and Structured Evidence Synthesis (SES), using a proposed Token-Accuracy Ratio (TAR) to capture the trade-off between accuracy and token cost. Centralized governance with instructor-led participation and instructor-curated summarization reportedly reduces token costs by up to 93.0% while maintaining even better accuracy. Decentralized systems showed higher variance and computational inefficiency, particularly on SES, where misaligned agents degraded performance. Stated limitations include dependence on the quality and completeness of contextual data, possible coordination and efficiency challenges as agent counts grow, the assumption that agents interpret context independently, uncertain generalization beyond the specific tasks, no integration of external knowledge, and difficulty tracing the rationale behind agent interactions.
